Sub.: Notice of 25th Annual General Meeting and Integrated Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26 
Ref.: Regulation 30 and 34 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 
 
 
Dear Sir / Madam, 
 
In continuation to our earlier intimation dated June 19, 2026, we wish to inform that Twenty-Fifth (25th) Annual General Meeting 
(“AGM”) of members of the Company will be held on Thursday, July 30, 2026 at 10.30 am (IST) through video conference / other 
audio-visual means, in accordance with the applicable circulars issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (“MCA”) and the 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”). 
 
In this regard, we hereby submit the following: 
 
 Notice convening 25th AGM 
 Integrated Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26 
 
The aforesaid documents are being sent through e-mail to those members of the Company whose e-mail addresses are registered 
with the Company/ Registrar to an Issue & Share Transfer Agent (i.e. MUFG Intime India Private Limited) (“RTA”)/ Depository 
Participant(s) (“DP”), in accordance with the relevant circulars issued by MCA and SEBI and are also available on Company’s 
website at www.maxhealthcare.in/investors/corporategovernance/general-meetings-and-postal-ballot.  
 
Further, in terms of regulation 36(1)(b) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, a letter 
containing the web-link, exact path and QR Code comprising the complete details of Notice convening 25th AGM and  
Integrated Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26, is being sent to those members who have not registered their e-mail 
address with the Company/ RTA/ DP.  A copy of letter that is being dispatched to members is enclosed as Annexure. 
 
This disclosure will also be hosted on Company's website viz. www.maxhealthcare.in.  
 
Kindly take the same on record. 
 
Thanking you 
 
Yours truly,  
 
For Max Healthcare Institute Limited

Explanatory Statement
In accordance with the provisions of Section 102 of 
the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Companies Act”) read 
with Regulation 36 and other applicable provisions of 
the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 
(“SEBI Listing Regulations”), the following explanatory 
statement forms part of this Notice.
Although an explanatory statement is not required under 
the Companies Act for the Ordinary Business set out at 
Item Nos. 1 to 4 of this Notice, the Company has, as a measure 
of good corporate governance and for the benefit of its 
Members, voluntarily provided the following information:
Item Nos. 1 and 2
Pursuant to the provisions of Section 129 of the Companies 
Act read with the Rules made thereunder, the audited 
standalone and consolidated financial statements of every 
company are required to be laid before the members at every 
annual general meeting for their consideration and adoption. 
Further, Section 134 of the Companies Act requires that the 
report of the board of directors and the report of the statutory 
auditors shall be attached to the financial statements.
The Board of Directors of the Company (“Board”), at its 
meeting held on May 21, 2026, upon the recommendation 
of the Audit Committee, approved the Audited Standalone 
and Consolidated Financial Statements for the financial 
year ended March 31, 2026. The Company’s financial and 
operational performance, together with the key developments 
during the financial year, is presented in various sections of 
the Integrated Annual Report including the Board’s Report, 
the Management Discussion and Analysis and the Financial 
Capital section.
The Audited Standalone and Consolidated Financial 
Statements, together with the Board’s Report and the Statutory 
Auditors’ Reports thereon, form part of the Integrated Annual 
Report for financial year 2025-26 circulated to the Members 
and are also available on the website of the Company.  
The Statutory Auditors of the Company, M/s S.R. Batliboi & 
Co. LLP, Chartered Accountants, have issued an unmodified 
audit opinion on both the Standalone and Consolidated 
Financial 
Statements 
for 
the 
financial 
year 
ended 
March 31, 2026. The Auditors’ Reports do not contain any 
qualification, reservation, adverse remark or disclaimer. 
The Standalone and Consolidated Financial Statements have 
been prepared in accordance with the applicable provisions 
of the Companies Act, the Indian Accounting Standards 
(Ind AS) and other applicable accounting principles and 
present a true and fair view of the financial position and 
financial performance of the Company.
The Members desirous of seeking any information or 
clarification in relation to the Standalone or Consolidated 
Financial Statements are requested to send their queries to 
the Chief Financial Officer at CFO@maxhealthcare.com on 
or before Sunday, July 26, 2026, to enable the management 
to respond appropriately at the 25th Annual General Meeting. 
The Board recommends the Ordinary Resolutions set out at 
Item Nos. 1 and 2 of this Notice for approval by the Members.
None of the Directors or Key Managerial Personnel of 
the Company or their respective relatives is, in any way, 
concerned or interested, financially or otherwise, in the 
resolutions set out at Item Nos. 1 and 2, except to the extent 
of their respective shareholding, if any, in the Company.
Item No. 3
Pursuant to the provisions of Section 123 of the Companies 
Act, the members of a company may approve the final 
dividend at their annual general meeting, upon the 
recommendation of the board of directors of the company. 
Further, in accordance with the Dividend Distribution Policy 
of the Company, the Board of Directors (“Board”) may 
propose/ declare dividends up to 40% of profits after tax 
of the Company while aiming to recommend a minimum 
of 10% of the face value of share annually. In extraordinary 
circumstances, a higher payout may be declared.
The Board, at its meeting held on May 21, 2026, after 
considering 
the 
Company’s 
financial 
performance, 
profitability, cash flows, capital expenditure requirements, 
future/ strategic growth plans, overall financial position and 
benchmarking against peer companies, recommended a 
final dividend of ₹2/- (20% of the face value) per equity share 
of ₹10/- each for the financial year ended March 31, 2026. 
The recommended dividend is higher than the final dividend 
of ₹1.50 per equity share declared for the previous financial 
year ended March 31, 2025.
The recommended dividend represents a payout ratio of 
~27.2% of the standalone profit after tax for the financial 
year ended March 31, 2026 reflecting the Company’s 
commitment to providing sustainable returns to the Members 
while retaining adequate resources to fund the Company’s 
growth strategy, capital expenditure requirements and other 
business needs.
Subject to the approval of the Members, the final dividend 
will be paid to those Members whose names appear 
in the Register of Members or in the records of the 
depositories as beneficial owners as on the Record Date, i.e. 
Friday, July 3, 2026, within the timelines prescribed under 
the Companies Act and other applicable laws.
The Board recommends the Ordinary Resolution set out at 
Item No. 3 of this Notice for approval by the Members.
None of the Directors or Key Managerial Personnel of 
the Company or their respective relatives is, in any way, 
concerned or interested, financially or otherwise, in the 
resolution set out at Item No. 3, except to the extent of their 
entitlement to receive dividend as Members of the Company, 
if any.

Proposal
The Company follows a robust and structured process for 
appointment and re-appointment of Board Members. The 
Nomination and Remuneration Committee (“NRC”) oversees 
Board succession planning and evaluates, inter-alia, the 
background, experience, skill set, performance, educational 
& professional qualification, integrity, independence of 
judgement, time commitment and overall contribution of 
Directors. The Board also considers its overall composition 
including balance between Executive and Non-Executive 
Directors, diversity, tenure and alignment with the Board 
approved Skill Matrix. 
The NRC, at its meeting held on March 17, 2026, while 
reviewing 
the 
Board 
succession 
plan, 
noted 
that 
Mr Anil Kumar Bhatnagar had attained the age of 
75 (seventy-five) years on August 14, 2025 and that the 
Members had, on July 30, 2025, approved his continuation 
as a Director beyond the age of 75 years by way of a Special

We believe the future of healthcare 
will be increasingly integrated, 
personalised, and accessible beyond 
traditional hospital settings. Through 
Max@Home and Max Lab, we are 
extending our expertise directly into 
the communities we serve. Together, 
these businesses are strengthening 
accessibility and ensuring continuity of 
care beyond hospital infrastructure.
At Max Healthcare, advancing 
medicine requires not only  
world-class technology but also 
a strong commitment to research 
and learning. Through MIME and 
MIAPE, we continue to strengthen 
medical education and professional 
training, while our growing research 
ecosystem, comprising over 3,100 
published papers and 750+ active 
research grant projects, contributes 
meaningful clinical insights to the 
global healthcare community.
The legacy we continue to build is 
rooted in care, innovation, clinical 
excellence, and integrity. As we move 
into our next phase of growth, we 
remain committed to shaping the 
future of healthcare delivery in India 
through scale, technology, research, 
and patient-centred care. Yet, even 
as we continue to grow, one principle 
remains unchanged: patient care will 
always remain at the centre of every 
decision we make.
Pushing the 
Boundaries of 
Indian Healthcare
For Max Healthcare, pushing 
boundaries means continually 
advancing the standards of modern 
healthcare. Our pursuit takes shape 
by expanding access, strengthening 
infrastructure, embracing cutting-edge 
technology, and building capabilities 
that position us amongst the top 
integrated healthcare providers. 
Twenty-six years ago, we embarked 
on a mission to bring world-class 
healthcare closer to communities. That 
singular endeavour is now India’s most 
valuable listed healthcare organisation. 
Today, we are proud to operate a 
network of 21 healthcare facilities 
with over 6,000 beds, supported by a 
dedicated team of more than 40,000 
individuals. Our reach now extends 
across 800+ cities in India and 182 
countries worldwide. Yet, the true 
measure of our progress lies in the lives 
we touch. In FY 2025–26 alone, we 
cared for over 40 Lakh+ patients,  
with every patient interaction reflecting 
our commitment to compassionate, 
high-quality healthcare.
At the centre of this year’s theme is the 
strong momentum driving our growth 
journey. From the successful launch of 
Max Dwarka to the commencement of 
operations at the new towers in  
Max Smart, Saket (Delhi), Max Mohali, 
and Nanavati Max Mumbai, we 
continue to strengthen our presence 
through strategic infrastructure 
expansion. With upcoming 
developments across Lucknow, 
Nagpur, Zirakpur, Pitampura, Dwarka, 
Vaishali, Dehradun, Thane and 
Pune, we are further expanding 
our healthcare network to serve 
more communities. Together, these 
developments support our vision of 
doubling bed capacity over the next 
five years and building one of India’s 
most advanced healthcare networks.
Our physical expansion is closely 
aligned with our focus on clinical and 
digital transformation. We continue 
to invest in advanced technologies, 
including 42 robotic systems such 
as Da Vinci and EDGE machines, to 
enhance precision, efficiency, and 
patient outcomes across our hospitals.
Our progress continues to be guided 
by a strong foundation of governance, 
ethics, and institutional excellence. 
Institutional Investor Advisory Services 
India Limited (IiAS) recognised us 
as a ‘Next Leader’, for the second 
consecutive year, placing us amongst 
the top 20 companies in the S&P  
BSE100 Index for corporate 
governance. At the same time, being 
recognised as a Great Place to Work® 
(GPTW) for the fourth consecutive year 
reflects our commitment to fostering 
a culture of trust, collaboration, and 
professional growth.
At Max Healthcare, our responsibility 
extends beyond clinical care. 
Through the Max Medical Scholarship 
Programme, we have funded the 
complete medical education of  
245 meritorious students from 
financially weaker communities, 
helping nurture the next generation 
of healthcare professionals. We also 
remain committed to ensuring that 
financial limitations do not become 
barriers to quality treatment. In the 
last financial year, we provided 
over `244.30 Crore in free medical 
treatment to approximately  
3.60 Lakh patients, enabling access to 
compassionate, quality healthcare  
for underserved communities.
The theme of our Integrated Annual Report for FY 2025–26, 
‘Pushing the Boundaries of Indian Healthcare’, demonstrates 
our drive to transform healthcare delivery through clinical 
excellence, innovation, and compassionate patient care.

Risk Management Process
To support the governance structure, Max Healthcare follows a continuous and disciplined risk management process.  
This ensures that risk management is not a periodic exercise but an ongoing cycle embedded in day-to-day operations.
The process begins with identification of risk across clinical and non-clinical areas, followed by structured assessment based 
on likelihood impact and control effectiveness. Once risks are prioritised, mitigation plans are developed with clear ownership 
and timelines. Risk Management Policy & Risk Appetite guidance note also supports the management in such prioritisation & 
mitigation plan management. These plans are then monitored continuously, with periodic reassessments to reflect evolving 
conditions. Where necessary, material risks are escalated to the appropriate governance bodies for review and direction. 
Through this cycle, the Company ensures that risks are actively managed, rather than retrospectively addressed.
Key Risks and Mitigation Strategies 
Within this framework, the Company identifies and tracks key risks across critical areas of the business. Each category reflects a 
distinct set of exposures, along with targeted measures designed to manage their impact and sustain operational stability.

Double Materiality Assessment 
Measuring Impact 
Both Ways
Regular materiality assessments form the bedrock of 
sound business and sustainability strategy, helping identify 
the issues that matter most to the organisation and its 
stakeholders. Max Healthcare takes this a step further through 
a Double Materiality Assessment (DMA), which recognises the 
inseparable link between impact and financial performance. 
The DMA evaluates two distinct yet interconnected lenses:
Impact Materiality takes an inside-out 
view, evaluating the organisation’s 
influence on environmental, social and 
societal factors, including assessing 
the impact of operations on community 
health outcomes, environmental 
stewardship and the value chain. 
Financial Materiality adopts an 
outside-in lens, examining how 
external factors, such as governance 
practices, economic performance 
and business continuity, may present 
risks or opportunities that could affect 
future cash flows and long-term value 
creation.
Max Healthcare conducted its DMA in 
FY 2023–24 and continues to apply 
the same framework. The assessment 
is reviewed every three to four years 
to ensure continued alignment with 
evolving regulations, stakeholder 
expectations and market dynamics, 
with outcomes approved by senior 
management and the ESG and 
Sustainability Committee.
The Double Materiality Assessment 
has been reviewed and endorsed 
by the Board as a strategic input 
to strategic planning, enterprise 
risk management and stakeholder 
engagement. ESG and Sustainability 
Committee at the Board level 
continues to monitor progress against 
material sustainability priorities and 
oversee the integration of these 
considerations into governance, 
operations and long-term business 
strategy, on a bi-annual basis.
Embedding Materiality 
into Enterprise Risk 
Management 
Max Healthcare has integrated 
material ESG topics directly into its 
Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) 
framework, ensuring sustainability 
risks are identified, assessed 
and managed alongside broader 
business risks. A formal ERM review 
is conducted every six months, 
bringing together risk owners, Chief 
Risk Officers and the Risk Committee 
to collectively review and validate 
the enterprise-wide risk register. 
Sustainability-related risks are 
assigned to designated owners for 
continuous monitoring and mitigation, 
strengthening risk oversight and 
supporting informed decision-making 
across the organisation.
Stakeholder Groups 
Engaged in the DMA 
Max Healthcare engaged with its key 
stakeholder groups to ensure their 
insights and concerns were central to 
the DMA process and reflected in the 
priorities identified.
DMA Process 
1
Identification of  
Material Topics
A preliminary broad set of 
ESG topics was identified 
through peer benchmarking 
and reference to global 
frameworks.
2
Shortlisting of  
Material Topics
The identified topics were 
screened based on their 
relevance to business 
operations and stakeholder 
importance.
3
Business-wise  
Consultation and 
Prioritisation
Shortlisted topics were 
thereafter evaluated 
through stakeholder 
consultations and prioritised 
using defined criteria such 
as impact severity and 
business relevance.
4
Final List of  
Material Topics
The prioritised topics were 
validated by leadership and 
consolidated into a final 
set of material issues to 
be integrated into strategy 
and disclosures.

data collection.

relevant information into their 
workflows. Since deployment, the

scalability across specialities further 
strengthens its value as a 
network-wide clinical productivity tool.

Case Study
Patients seeking medical help often 
describe their symptoms using 
simple, everyday words instead 
of medical jargon. Traditional 
keyword-based search systems 
struggle to understand this kind 
of input, leading to ineffective 
results and delays in finding the 
right specialist. This issue is even 
more pronounced in a multilingual 
country, where patients may speak 
regional languages or use mixed-
language phrases.
Max Healthcare addressed this 
gap by developing an AI-powered 
Symptom Search capability that 
allows patients to describe their 
symptoms naturally, in multiple 
languages. The system interprets 
inputs across multiple Indian 
languages and dialects, translating 
them into structured clinical 
insights and mapping them to the 
appropriate medical specialities. The 
solution leverages healthcare-tuned 
language models that understand 
clinical context and the relationships 
between symptoms and conditions. 
The system uses this information 
to guide patients towards the right 
care pathway even when symptoms 
are described imprecisely or across 
multiple conditions.
Since its launch, the feature has 
been widely adopted, with many 
users turning to it for sensitive 
health issues, indicating growing 
trust in digital health platforms. It 
highlights the value of intuitive, 
inclusive tools that make care 
more accessible. By allowing users 
to navigate accurately without 
medical expertise, the initiative 
has enhanced accessibility and 
helped reduce delays in receiving 
proper treatment.

Case Study
Automated Prototype for Measurements of Angles and Lengths in Whole 
Lower Limb Hip-Knee-Ankle (HKA) Radiographs — A Joint Patent by Max 
Healthcare and IIT Bombay
Accurate assessment of lower-limb 
length and alignment is critical for 
the diagnosis and surgical planning 
of patients with knee osteoarthritis. 
These assessments use 
radiographs (X-rays) to capture 
images of the entire lower limb, 
from the hip to the ankle, in a 
standing position for diagnostic 
evaluation. These radiographs 
are routinely performed in the 
radiology department for patients, 
either by a radiologist familiar with 
these measurements or by the 
orthopaedic surgeon performing the 
surgery. Since this is a subjective 
assessment and general radiologists 
may be unfamiliar with the methods 
for taking these measurements, 
there is variability in the reporting 
of such radiographs, leading to 
inconsistencies and errors. Such 
discrepancies affect the accuracy 
of the surgery.
To address this challenge, Max 
Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, 
launched an initiative in December 
2023, led by Dr Bharat Agarwal, 
Principal Director, Radiology, in 
collaboration with IIT Bombay. 
The project focused on building an 
automated tool that uses computer 
vision and artificial intelligence 
techniques to obtain these 
measurements, providing consistent 
and reproducible results. 
The tool was designed to help reduce 
measurement time, improve the 
consistency and reproducibility of 
lower-limb alignment measurements, 
and create a standardised presentation 
of radiographic results for the 
orthopaedic surgeon and the patient. 
It also eliminated inter-observer 
variability by producing standardised 
outputs regardless of the reporting 
clinician’s sub-speciality experience 
and it seamlessly integrates with 
existing PACS infrastructure. These 
improvements provided accurate 
information to plan total knee 
arthroplasty surgeries, with the 
potential to reduce postoperative 
mal-alignment, revision rates, 
and associated patient morbidity.
Key Outcomes
•	 The system demonstrated 
clinical accuracy of 96.9% for 
angular measurements 
(within ±1°) and 96.0% for length 
measurements (within ±2mm), 
validated against expert 
musculoskeletal radiologists 
across a cohort of 279 patients 
with diverse pathologies. Mean 
angular deviation was just 
0.3° ± 0.8°, and mean length 
deviation was 0.8mm ± 1.1mm. 
•	 Over 83% of patients achieved 
complete agreement on both 
measurement categories. 
Measurement time was 
reduced by approximately 
95%, from 20–25 minutes 
manually to under one minute.

partnerships, please refer to the 
section on Healthcare Partnerships 
on number page 127 of this report.

BMR-5000 Robotic Surgery System for Superior Patient Experience
Traditional open surgery continues 
to present challenges such as 
larger incisions, greater blood 
loss, longer hospital stays, higher 
infection risk, and extended 
recovery times. On the other hand, 
minimally invasive conventional 
techniques like laparoscopy can 
face limitations due to reduced 
precision, restricted range of 
movement and high dependency 
on surgeon skill in complex 
procedures. Hence, there is an 
opportunity for next-generation 
surgical technologies to improve 
clinical precision, safety and 
patient recovery.
Max Super Speciality Hospital, Vaishali, in collaboration with Maulana Azad 
Medical College, New Delhi, conducted the world’s first clinical study in humans 
to assess the safety and efficacy of the BMR-5000 robotic surgery system for 
general surgeries. The study, initiated on October 5, 2024 and completed on 
November 25, 2025, was led by Dr Vivek Bindal, Senior Director and Head of 
Minimal Access, Bariatric and Robotic Surgery, with Dr Pawanindra Lal serving 
as the coordinating investigator.
Key Outcomes
A total of 60 patients were enrolled in the study, in which the use of 
the BMR-5000 system was monitored, and it showed a 100% surgical 
success rate with no major complications. The BMR-5000 effectively 
performed critical surgical functions such as tissue clamping, 
dissection, suturing, haemostasis, digestive tract reconstruction, 
nerve exposure, and protection. The system also met the expected 
safety and effectiveness standards. This landmark study provides 
important clinical evidence for the potential of robotic surgery 
to improve precision and outcomes in minimally invasive care.

recombinant Hepatitis E vaccine 
in healthy adults and adolescents. 
The study began in July 2021 and 
was completed on June 20, 2023, 
with the vaccine launched in 
September 2025.

Data Security  
and Privacy 
Max Healthcare maintains a 
comprehensive cybersecurity and 
data privacy framework, underpinned 
by a robust Cybersecurity Policy. This 
is further supported by responsive 
governance structures to ensure 
effective implementation across 
the organisation. A dedicated team 
oversees privacy and data protection, 
with cybersecurity embedded into 
the overall risk and compliance 
management framework to enable 
proactive identification, monitoring, 
and mitigation of cyber risks. Regular 
training sessions and awareness 
programmes are held for employees 
to boost their understanding of 
cybersecurity best practices, 
responsible data management, and 
strategies to prevent breaches and 
cyber threats.
MHIL demonstrates a strict 
zero-tolerance stance toward 
cybersecurity breaches by 
implementing accountability 
measures, including disciplinary 
actions for violations of cybersecurity 
protocols. To boost organisational 
resilience, a cybersecurity crisis 
management plan is in place, which is 
periodically reviewed and updated to 
enhance preparedness and incident 
response capabilities.
The effectiveness of this governance-
led approach is reflected in the 
Company’s performance during  
FY 2025–26. The Company reported 
zero cybersecurity incidents, received 
zero complaints from external parties, 
organisations, or regulatory bodies 
regarding customer privacy breaches 
and recorded zero identified cases of 
customer data leaks, theft, or loss.
Governance 
The Risk Management Committee 
and the Information System Security 
Committee at MHIL oversee 
cybersecurity strategy. These 
committees ensure governance, 
accountability, and continuous 
monitoring of cybersecurity risks 
and initiatives through internal and 
external audits.
The governance structure 
incorporates the Confidentiality, 
Integrity, and Availability (CIA) and 
Factor Analysis of Information  
Risk (FAIR). This combination 
allows for more precise cyber risk 
assessment and enhances support 
for business continuity.
Vulnerability 
Assessments
The Company conducts vulnerability 
assessments and simulates cyber-
attack scenarios, including phishing, 
ransomware, and vishing. This 
helps evaluate the effectiveness 
of its information security controls 
and employee awareness. The 
process involves defining the 
scope, designing attack scenarios, 
executing controlled simulations, 
monitoring detection and response, 
and analysing results to identify 
vulnerabilities and control gaps.  
The assessment evaluates employee 
susceptibility to social engineering, 
effectiveness of security controls 
such as email and endpoint 
protection, and reporting and 
escalation practices. Findings are 
reviewed by the Information Security 
team, and corrective actions and 
training are initiated to strengthen 
awareness, reinforce policy adoption, 
and deploy advanced technical 
solutions.
During the financial year, a 
comprehensive third-party audit 
was conducted covering the 
Company’s IT infrastructure and 
application landscape across 20 
healthcare facilities. The audit 
included Vulnerability Assessment 
and Penetration Testing (VAPT) 
across in-scope systems, covering 
areas such as OT environment, 
cloud security, active directory, and 
security configuration reviews across 
multiple locations and critical assets. 
All observations identified during the 
audit were subsequently addressed 
and closed within the reporting period.
Employee  
Engagement and 
Awareness Training 
All employees are required to 
undergo information security and 
cybersecurity awareness training to 
build an understanding of potential 
threat scenarios and the importance 
of safeguarding organisational 
information. This includes awareness 
sessions during onboarding, periodic 
refresher training, and regular 
communications covering topics such 
as simulation attacks, cybersecurity 
risks, data protection responsibilities, 
phishing, ransomware, safe internet 
usage, password security, and data 
protection practices. Employees 
are also encouraged to report any 
suspicious activity or potential 
security incidents to the Information 
Security team, as part of the 
Company’s all-pervasive vigilance 
and responsibility.

critical to MHIL’s approach to delivering

embedded privacy controls across its 
digital ecosystem, including securing 
enterprise applications such as 
Hospital Information Systems (HIS) 
and Electronic Medical Records (EMR) 
to ensure data is handled securely 
and in compliance with regulations. 
Key initiatives include adopting 
a Privacy by Design approach, 
where privacy controls are built into 
systems from the outset. Centralised 
data discovery tools help identify 
and classify personally identifiable 
information (PII), while a standardised 
consent framework ensures that 
data shared with third parties is 
transparent, lawful, and traceable. 
Max Healthcare’s dedicated Data 
Privacy Office has an ongoing focus 
on risk assessment, training, and 
building resilience to maintain high 
standards of data protection.
DPDPA Implementation 
Roadmap
Max Healthcare is advancing its 
DPDA journey through a structured 
implementation roadmap, with a 
current focus on high-impact areas. 
The Company has set up a dedicated 
Data Privacy office along with 
defined data retention schedules 
and organisational and technical 
controls. Any personal data breaches 
are managed in accordance with 
DPDPA requirements. All suspected 
or actual breaches must be reported 
immediately to the DPO. Breaches 
are contained, assessed for impact, 
and documented. Where required, 
the Data Protection Board of India 
and affected individuals are notified 
within prescribed timelines. The 
Company ensures that the ‘Privacy 
Incident and Personal Data Breach 
Management’ procedure is followed 
in the event of any personal data 
breach.
Max Healthcare has a well-defined 
rule for managing personal data, 
supported by a data retention and 
archival policy framework. The 
duration of data retention is only 
until the fulfilment of its intended 
purpose or as required by statutory 
obligations. Defined retention 
schedules apply to different 
categories of data (e.g., lifelong 
retention for critical care records; 
defined retention periods for general 
medical records; steps undertaken 
for the retention of general medical 
records; statutory periods for 
employee and vendor data). The 
Company has adopted a ‘Policy 
for Preservation of Documents and 
Archiving of Documents’ to ensure 
that records are systematically 
archived, safeguarded, and are 
retrievable for future reference, in line 
with legal, regulatory, and operational 
needs. Once retention periods expire, 
data is securely disposed of through 
approved methods such as digital 
wiping or physical shredding.
Efforts are also underway to improve 
visibility and control over personal 
data through automated discovery 
and classification tools for managing 
sensitive information. The Company 
is also adopting a more robust 
consent ecosystem, with workflows 
being developed to manage consent 
collection, usage, and withdrawal in a 
transparent and compliant manner.
MHIL’s employees, contractors, and 
relevant third parties are regularly 
trained on privacy and data protection 
obligations. Mandatory training is

Max Healthcare’s Clinical and Operational Resilience Framework
The Company’s Service Continuity 
Plan operationalises this framework 
by defining hospital-wide response 
protocols for fire and non-fire 
emergencies, including waterlogging 
or flooding, medical gas disruption, 
mass casualities, pandemic and 
earthquakes. The plan outlines 
clear responsibilities across hospital 
leadership, emergency services, 
medical administration, nursing, 
ambulance services, engineering 
and biomedical engineering teams. 
It provides for alternate sources of 
electricity, water and medical gases, 
use of portable equipment, rapid 
restoration of damaged infrastructure, 
and coordination with other healthcare 
facilities within the Max Healthcare 
network and nearby healthcare 
facilities where required.
A key feature of the plan is its patient-
centred approach to continuity of 
care. In situations involving capacity 
constraints, the plan provides for 
ICU and ward-level prioritisation, 
temporary holding arrangements 
and transfer of patients only after 
assessing clinical stability, risk and 
the ability of the receiving facility to 
meet the patient’s needs. For critical 
and unstable patients, the plan 
emphasises medical supervision, 
appropriate ambulance support, 
life-support equipment, transfer 
documentation, informed consent 
and continuous monitoring during 
movement. This ensures that 
emergency response remains clinically 
governed and aligned with patient 
safety requirements.
Recognising the increasing 
dependence of healthcare delivery on 
digital systems, Max Healthcare has 
integrated IT Disaster Recovery into 
its business continuity approach. The 
Company’s IT continuity framework 
covers business-critical clinical and 
enterprise applications, including 
health information systems, electronic 
medical records, laboratory and 
radiology systems, patient record 
systems, billing, HRMS, identity 
and access systems, document 
repositories, network infrastructure 
and third-party managed applications. 
The framework is designed to 
address technology disruptions 
arising from system outages, cyber 
incidents, infrastructure failures, data 
corruption, vendor disruptions or 
physical events affecting information 
processing facilities.
Max Healthcare’s IT Disaster 
Recovery approach is built around 
defined business impact analysis, 
risk prioritisation, recovery objectives 
and continuity strategies for 
critical ICT services. The Company 
maintains a combination of high-
availability configurations, disaster 
recovery environments, periodic 
data replication, backup verification, 
redundant network components, 
secure access mechanisms and 
documented manual fallback 
workflows. These measures are 
intended to support continuity of 
clinical and operational processes 
such as patient admission, diagnostics, 
prescriptions, billing, reporting, payroll 
and internal communications during 
technology disruptions.
The IT DR governance structure 
establishes defined roles for the CIO, 
Information Security and Governance 
function, IT infrastructure teams, 
application owners, database 
administrators, cybersecurity 
teams, departmental IT leads 
and relevant business functions. 
Escalation protocols are aligned 
to incident severity, ranging from 
local system issues and application-
level disruptions to infrastructure-
wide outages, patient care risks, 
compliance impacts and extended 
disruptions requiring executive 
oversight. This structure enables 
coordinated decision-making across 
technology, clinical, administrative, 
vendor and security stakeholders 
during an incident.
The Disaster Recovery process also 
provides a structured pathway for 
safe restoration of IT services once 
business operations have been 
stabilised. This includes validation 
of incident resolution, assessment 
of primary infrastructure readiness, 
reconciliation of data changes 
created during the recovery period, 
alignment of configurations, controlled 
switch-back from disaster recovery 
environments to production systems, 
user acceptance testing, verification 
of cybersecurity controls and post-
restoration monitoring. Evidence of 
recovery actions, system validations, 
deviations and business-owner sign-
offs is retained to support auditability 
and continuous improvement.
Max Healthcare also conducts 
structured BCP and DR testing to 
validate readiness. The testing 
approach includes tabletop exercises, 
cybersecurity simulations, controlled 
failover testing for business-
critical applications, validation of 
recovery objectives and review 
of escalation workflows. Tests are 
planned through approved test 
calendars and, wherever required, 
are performed in isolated test or 
disaster recovery environments 
using masked or pseudonymised 
data to protect sensitive patient 
and business information. Post-test 
debriefs, corrective action plans 
and management reviews are used 
to capture lessons learned and 
strengthen future resilience.
Max Healthcare has also strengthened 
its preparedness for public health 
emergencies through an Emergency 
Management Programme for Global 
Communicable Diseases. The 
programme establishes a structured 
response system for emerging 
infectious disease threats, including 
defined activation triggers, infection 
surveillance, screening at points of 
entry, triage, isolation, emergency 
staffing, supply management, 
visitor control and surge capacity 
planning. It also provides for internal 
communication with staff and external 
reporting to relevant public health 
authorities, while aligning response 
protocols with applicable national and 
international health guidance.
Through synergised efforts, these 
plans reflect Max Healthcare’s 
integrated approach to clinical, 
operational and digital resilience. By 
combining risk assessment, command 
structures, critical infrastructure 
continuity, IT disaster recovery, safe 
patient management, workforce and 
supply preparedness, cybersecurity 
readiness, stakeholder communication 
and periodic drills, the Company is 
strengthening its ability to deliver safe, 
reliable and responsive care even 
during periods of uncertainty.

Supply Chain Management 
Maintaining a responsible and 
responsive supply chain is essential 
to ensuring clinical excellence and 
patient safety by ensuring the timely 
availability of life-saving drugs, 
medical consumables, and advanced 
equipment. A responsible value chain 
also incorporates ethical sourcing and 
strict quality standards, helping reduce 
risks associated with substandard 
materials and non-compliance. 
MHIL maintains a responsible value 
chain by partnering with suppliers 
who uphold high standards of ethics, 
integrity, and compliance across their 
operations, ensuring operational 
efficiency and service quality. The 
Supplier Code of Conduct sets the 
foundation for environmental, social, 
and governance (ESG) accountability 
across the value chain.
The Company’s operational agility 
and continuity are facilitated by the 
close integration of its procurement 
and clinical teams and backed by 
advanced inventory management 
systems for real-time tracking of 
goods, significantly minimising manual 
processes. This tech-driven approach 
improves demand forecasting, 
ensuring that critical medical supplies 
are always available while driving 
cost-efficiency through lean inventory 
practices. 
Max Healthcare undertakes regular 
assessments and has structured 
planning cycles so suppliers can 
deliver materials and equipment 
to match clinical schedules. This 
ensures that patient care remains 
uninterrupted due to any supply 
shortages, and at the same time, 
there are no inefficiencies from 
overstocking.
MHIL recognises that delivering 
quality patient care depends on 
capabilities beyond its hospitals to 
a broader ecosystem of suppliers 
and service partners. To strengthen 
this ecosystem, the Company is 
progressively integrating ESG 
considerations into procurement 
practices through contractual 
provisions, supplier declarations, and 
risk-based engagement mechanisms. 
Adopting this approach enables Max 
Healthcare to maintain a transparent, 
resilient, compliant, and sustainable 
value chain. 
Supplier Screening 
Suppliers are screened based on 
the level of risk the products and 
services pose to patients, employees, 
and operations. They are evaluated 
on criticality, share of procurement 
spend, regulatory exposure, and 
potential impact on patient safety 
and service continuity. Based on this, 
each significant supplier is placed in a 
high-, medium-, or low-risk category, 
which then determines the intensity of 
engagement that follows. Screening 
parameters align with SEBI’s BRSR 
Core principles and cover  
ESG dimensions relevant to a 
healthcare operator. 
•	 On the environmental side, 
the focus is on biomedical 
waste handling, storage and 
transportation of hazardous 
materials, energy performance of 
equipment supplied, responsible 
resource use, and compliance 
with environmental laws. 
•	 On the social side, screening 
looks at occupational health 
and safety, statutory labour 
compliance, prevention of 
child and forced labour, fair 
employment conditions within 
outsourced services, employee 
welfare, and respect for  
human rights. 
•	 On governance, the review 
covers business ethics, regulatory 
track record, transparency in 
operations, and the overall 
maturity of management systems. 
The assessment findings help 
determine which suppliers may be 
onboarded and which need a closer 
ESG review. 
Supplier Assessment  
and Development 
Building on the screening 
framework, MHIL is developing a 
structured supplier ESG assessment 
methodology that combines desk-
based evaluations with risk-informed 
verification mechanisms. The 
methodology references applicable 
national healthcare regulations, labour 
standards, environmental standards, 
and recognised management system 
frameworks such as ISO certifications 
where relevant. 
Supplier ESG assessments evaluate:
•	 Environmental management 
practices
•	 Occupational health and safety 
systems
•	 Ethical sourcing safeguards
•	 Labour compliance mechanisms
•	 Governance maturity
For high-risk and operationally critical 
suppliers, MHIL plans to progressively 
introduce independent third-party 
verification mechanisms over 
subsequent implementation phases. 
Beyond assessment, the Company 
is adopting a development-oriented 
engagement approach to enhance 
suppliers’ capabilities and align them 
with the Company’s sustainability 
goals through guidance, awareness 
sessions, and improvement pathways. 
KPIs for Supplier Screening 
and Assessment Coverage 
Max Healthcare has initiated the 
classification of significant Tier 1 
suppliers across key categories such 
as pharmaceuticals, consumables, 
diagnostics, and facility management. 
A KPI framework is being developed to 
track ESG screening and assessment 
coverage, including the proportion 
of suppliers screened, assessed, 
and categorised by risk, along with 
procurement spend coverage. 
These metrics will strengthen the 
Company’s BRSR Core disclosures and 
enable more structured reporting in 
subsequent years. 
Internal systems are being built to 
monitor the extent to which the 
significant supplier base is screened 
against defined ESG parameters. The 
KPI framework being developed is 
expected to track: 
•	 The number and share of 
significant suppliers screened on 
ESG parameters 
•	 The number and share of 
significant suppliers taken through 
a detailed ESG assessment 
•	 The share of procurement 
spend represented by screened 
suppliers 
•	 The distribution of significant 
suppliers across high, medium, 
and low risk categories

Climate Risk Exposure
Max Healthcare’s assets span multiple urban locations, each with varying levels of exposure to climate-related risks. Scenario 
analysis indicates that certain geographies are more vulnerable due to factors such as rising temperatures, changing 
precipitation patterns, and water stress, which can affect operations and infrastructure performance. 
The findings from this analysis, based on multiple future climate scenarios, are presented below:

Temperature Risk
Hospitals in Delhi NCR and 
Western Region (Nagpur) 
experience periods 
of high temperatures 
exceeding 40°C. This 
increase in temperature 
places additional load 
on HVAC systems and 
requires careful monitoring 
of medication storage 
conditions. Measures such 
as backup power and 
temperature mapping in 
pharmacies support safe 
storage and preparation 
of medicines in alignment 
with Joint Commission 
International (JCI) medication 
management standards.

Precipitation Risk
Heavy rainfall events in the 
Western Region (Mumbai 
and Nagpur) can lead to 
localised flooding, with the 
potential to affect logistics, 
power supply, and access 
routes. Flood preparedness 
measures, including 
drainage maintenance 
and provisions for 
biomedical waste storage, 
are incorporated within 
the Company’s Disaster 
Management Plan.

Climate Hazards
Urban flooding risks are 
prominent in locations 
such as the Western 
Region (Mumbai) and 
Delhi NCR, while exposure 
to seismic activity and 
cyclones remains relatively 
moderate in certain 
regions. Fire safety systems 
and hazardous waste 
management practices are 
integrated into emergency 
response protocols and 
facility management plans 
to support operational 
continuity.

Water Scarcity

groundwater stress and 
variability in municipal 
water supply, which may

and sterilisation processes.

monitoring, and infection 
control practices help 
manage these risks in line 
with JCI infection prevention 
standards.

Case Study
Replacing Street Lighting with Solar Lights 
The electric pole lights at Max 
Super Speciality Hospital, Bathinda, 
had reached the end of their 
life, with many poles rusted and 
structurally damaged. Several 
peripheral areas experienced 
inadequate and unreliable 
illumination, especially at night, 
increasing the risk of accidents 
and security concerns such as 
theft or unauthorised activities. 
Maintenance challenges like 
ageing wiring, replacements and 
pole foundation limitations further 
affected the operations in the 
boundary area. 
To address these challenges, the 
hospital initiated a solar street 
lighting project between April 2025 
and September 2025. Building 
on the successful implementation 
of a 150 kWp onsite solar power 
plant for renewable electricity 
generation, the hospital further 
strengthened its clean energy 
infrastructure through additional 
renewable energy initiatives. As part 
of this initiative, 80 conventional grid-
based lighting systems were replaced 
with solar-powered alternatives to 
ensure reliable, energy-efficient, 
and sustainable outdoor illumination 
for enhanced safety and visibility 
across the premises. In addition, the 
new solar lighting system reduces 
dependence on conventional 
grid-based lighting and lowers 
maintenance requirements through 
the adoption of renewable energy 
solutions.
The system is equipped with 
remote control functionality to 
adjust light intensity (lux levels) 
based on operational requirements. 
Additionally, the solution also 
features a low-maintenance design, 
eliminating the need for extensive 
cabling and reducing infrastructure-
related challenges associated with 
traditional lighting systems.
Case Study
Agrivoltaics-based Solar Power Deployment
To promote the adoption of 
renewable energy without 
compromising agricultural 
productivity, the Government of 
Delhi has introduced an agrivoltaic 
framework that enables solar 
installations on active farmland. 
The model allows farming and 
clean energy generation to coexist, 
creating economic benefits 
for farmers while advancing 
sustainability objectives.
In alignment with this vision, 
Max Smart Super Speciality 
Hospital, Saket partnered with a 
renewable energy developer to 
source clean electricity from an 
agrivoltaic solar project established 
on agricultural land. Under this 
model, elevated solar panels have 
been installed above cultivated 
fields, enabling farmers to continue 
agricultural activities while generating 
additional rental income from the solar 
infrastructure installed on their land.
The renewable electricity generated 
through the project is supplied to the 
hospital, helping meet a portion of its 
energy requirements through clean 
energy sources. This arrangement 
creates shared value by providing 
farmers with a stable supplementary 
income stream, optimising 
land utilisation, and reducing 
dependence on conventional grid 
electricity, thereby supporting both 
environmental sustainability and 
rural economic development.

The partnership enables the sourcing of approximately 50 Lakh units of 
renewable electricity annually, resulting in estimated cost savings of H1.25 
Crore per year and a potential reduction of nearly 3,550 tCO₂e emissions. 
During the first five months of operation, the project supplied more than 
15 Lakh units of renewable electricity, delivering savings of approximately 
H37.50 Lakh while avoiding over 1,065 tCO₂e emissions. The model is 
planned to be replicated at the Saket East Block and Dwarka facility in the 
coming year.

Case Study
Pond Rejuvenation for Environment and Community Wellbeing in Kevli 
Village, Uttar Pradesh
Spread across 1.546 hectares, the 
Kevli village pond in the Lucknow 
district of Uttar Pradesh was 
severely degraded after nearly 20 
years of neglect. The pond was 
filled with silt, mud, and waste, 
leading to a complete loss of water 
storage and groundwater recharge 
capacity. Further, encroachments 
reduced its functional area, while 
stagnant polluted water contributed 
to mosquito breeding and 
associated health concerns. 
Max Healthcare collaborated with 
implementation partners and Kevli 
Gram Panchayat to undertake a 
comprehensive pond restoration 
project. The initiative aimed 
to restore the ecological and 
functional capacity of the village 
pond through a sustainable nature-
based water treatment process. 
It focused on improving water 
storage and groundwater recharge, 
water quality and biodiversity 
around the pond, as well as 
strengthening community stewardship 
for Max Healthcare. 
The process involved desiltation, 
deepening of the pond to ~20 feet, 
and removal of encroachments. 
A nature-based water treatment 
system, including constructed 
wetlands (root-zone treatment), 
anaerobic and facultative ponds, 
was implemented to ensure the 
natural purification of incoming water. 
Additional interventions included 
the plantation of over 300 trees, 
landscaping, installation of inlet and 
screening systems, fencing, lighting, 
and development of peripheral 
infrastructure to ensure long-term 
sustainability. The deployment of a 
nature-based constructed wetland 
system improved water quality, 
ensuring sustainable wastewater 
treatment and reducing the 
pollution load. The transformation 
of the site into a functional green 
space generated community 
goodwill, with active involvement 
of the Gram Panchayat and 
local self-help groups ensuring 
governance, ownership, and long-
term sustainability.
Impact Created
•	 Restored water holding capacity to ~26,168 m³ 
•	 Increased annual groundwater recharge of ~11,913 m³, strengthening 
local water security
•	 Mitigated public health risks by eliminating stagnant water and 
mosquito breeding
•	 Planted 300+ trees, which enhanced carbon sequestration potential, 
microclimate, and biodiversity conservation
Case Study
Restoration and Rejuvenation of Freshwater Pond in Mankrola Village, 
Gurugram District, Haryana
The freshwater pond at Mankrola 
village in Gurugram, Haryana, 
had deteriorated significantly 
due to unregulated dumping 
of solid waste, which adversely 
impacted water quality and 
disrupted the ecological balance. 
The Abhipsa Foundation, 
supported by Max Healthcare, 
undertook a comprehensive 
restoration and rejuvenation 
initiative between March 2025 
and July 2026, focusing on 
in-situ treatment and ecological 
enhancement of this pond.
The intervention incorporated 
in situ, nature-based solutions 
such as floating wetlands, 
phytoremediation, and the 
introduction of aquatic species. 
These measures improved water 
quality parameters, including 
pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), 
biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), 
chemical oxygen demand (COD), total 
dissolved solids (TDS), and nutrient 
levels. 
Additional measures included cleaning 
and levelling of the pond periphery, 
landscaping and horticultural 
enhancements, construction of a 
pedestrian walkway, and installation 
of fencing to prevent encroachment. 
Plantation of native trees and 
ornamental shrubs, and development 
of lighting and seating infrastructure 
were also implemented to enhance 
community usability and aesthetic 
value. The project benefited 
approximately 2,600 village 
residents, as well as an additional 
floating population of around 
1,000 people. The restored pond 
now functions as a sustainable 
ecological asset, supporting 
biodiversity conservation, carbon 
sequestration, and community 
development while ensuring long-
term environmental resilience.
Impact Created
•	 Rejuvenated pond improved storage capacity to approximately  
35,410 m³ (35.41 ML)
•	 Strengthened biodiversity through the plantation of 102 tree and 
shrub species, 530 ground cover plants, and the development of 
7,500 sq ft of grass cover
•	 Recorded a 2.3 m rise in water table with depth reducing from 4.7 m to 
2.4 m below ground level

Healthcare Infrastructure Gap Driving Capacity Expansion
India’s healthcare infrastructure remains significantly below global benchmarks, creating a strong structural growth opportunity 
for the sector. With an average of approximately 16 beds per 10,000 population as of FY 2024-25, compared to the global 
average of 33 and peers such as Brazil (25) and Thailand (24), the gap is further accentuated by the lower bed density of 
around 14 in non-metro regions. This shortfall, combined with rising disease burden and population growth, is driving sustained 
investments in capacity expansion and positioning infrastructure development as a key long-term growth driver for organised 
healthcare providers.

Changing Demographics and Disease Profile
India’s demographic profile is undergoing a structural shift, 
with the population aged 60+ projected to increase from 
10.5% in 2023 to approximately 12.6% by 2030, while the 
40–59 age group is expected to rise from 22.1% to 24.4%. 
This ageing trend, coupled with a rising incidence of non-
communicable diseases, is significantly increasing the 
demand for chronic disease management, geriatric care, 
and specialised healthcare services. Notably, around 66% 
of the elderly population has been reported to suffer from 
at least one chronic ailment, necessitating expansion and 
upgradation of healthcare infrastructure and services. 
Increasing Health Awareness and Rising Income Levels
Health awareness in India has improved significantly over 
the past decade, particularly among younger populations, 
driving greater adoption of preventive healthcare. At the 
same time, rising income levels are enhancing affordability 
and access to quality healthcare services. The share of 
households in the ₹1.5–2.0 lakh income bracket increased 
to approximately 40% in FY 2023-24, indicating improving 
purchasing power. Increasing urbanisation and literacy

across healthcare services.
Transition from Episodic to Continuum-of-Care Models
Healthcare delivery is expanding beyond episodic hospital-
based treatment into integrated, lifecycle-based care 
that includes diagnostics, homecare, rehabilitation, and 
preventive services. This is enhancing patient engagement 
and outcomes while opening additional revenue streams 
beyond inpatient care.
India’s Emergence as a Global Hub for Medical Tourism
India continues to strengthen its position as a global 
medical tourism destination, supported by advanced clinical 
capabilities, specialised medical expertise, and significantly 
lower treatment costs compared to developed markets. 
Key cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, 
and Hyderabad attract international patients seeking high-
quality care across complex procedures. India ranked 10th 
globally in the Medical Tourism Index (2020–21), reflecting 
its growing competitiveness.

Growing Health Insurance Coverage to Propel Demand
Health insurance coverage in India has increased from approximately 35% in FY 2018-19 to around 41% in FY 2024-25, with 
lives covered expanding from about 288 million individuals in FY 2014-15 to nearly 581 million in FY 2024-25. This shift from 
out-of-pocket spending to insurance-backed payment models is improving affordability, increasing hospitalisation rates, and 
driving demand for elective and planned procedures.
Industry estimates indicate that health insurance coverage is expected to further rise to around 45-50% by FY 2025-26, supported 
by growing healthcare awareness and wider participation from private insurers. As insured patient volumes increase, hospitals 
are increasingly engaging through institutional contracts, with evolving pricing dynamics and improved revenue visibility.

Opportunities
Max Healthcare’s growth trajectory is anchored in a clear, 
multi-pronged approach: expanding capacity organically, 
scaling through asset-light models, and pursuing disciplined 
inorganic growth initiatives. Underpinned by strong free cash 
flow generation, a prudent leverage profile and a proven 
execution track record, this approach enables the Company 
to capture rising demand while maintaining capital efficiency 
and industry-leading return on capital employed (ROCE).
The Company’s capital allocation framework emphasises 
disciplined growth, balance sheet prudence and return-
accretive deployment of capital. It continues to prioritise high-
return brownfield expansions and asset-light opportunities, 
while selectively pursuing greenfield projects in attractive 
catchments where demand fundamentals, clinical talent 
availability and long-term return potential are compelling. 
Inorganic growth remains an important lever, but pursued 
with strict valuation, integration and return thresholds. The 
Company intends to maintain net debt-to-EBITDA at not more 
than 2.5x, ensuring adequate flexibility to fund future growth 
opportunities while preserving balance sheet strength.

Diagnostics
The Indian diagnostics sector is expected to expand at 
a CAGR of approximately 12% over the next five years to 
reach an estimated USD 15–16 billion6. While diagnostics 
currently account for less than 10% of the overall healthcare 
industry in India, the segment remains a critical pillar of the 
care continuum, supporting early disease detection, clinical 
decision-making, preventive health management, and 
ongoing treatment monitoring.
Max Lab continued to scale its collection centre network 
across multiple cities during the year, supported by retail 
expansion, increased traction in the digital channel, and 
rising demand for speciality testing. Markets outside Delhi-
NCR, particularly Tier II cities, witnessed healthy growth 
aided by increasing adoption of wellness packages and 
preventive testing. To further enhance customer experience, 
the 
Company 
introduced 
several 
digital 
initiatives, 
including improved workflows in the customer application, 
real-time 
sample 
and 
phlebotomist 
tracking, 
and 
strengthened communication through the patient experience 
office. These interventions led to significant improvement in 
customer engagement and satisfaction.
Threats
Regulatory and Pricing Environment
A dynamic regulatory landscape continues to shape 
operating 
conditions 
across 
pricing, 
accreditation, 
compliance and cost structures. Expansion of price controls 
across consumables and diagnostics, along with revisions 
under government schemes such as CGHS and ECHS, 
may impact realisations and margins. Inflationary pressures 
on medical consumables, equipment, utilities, and other 
operating inputs could further affect cost efficiency. Changes 
in clinical protocols and accreditation requirements could 
also increase compliance costs. 
Response: The Company actively engages with industry 
bodies such as NATHEALTH, FICCI, and AHPI to represent 
industry perspectives, participate in policy discussions, and 
remain aligned with evolving regulatory requirements. It 
also continues to focus on procurement efficiencies, cost 
optimisation initiatives, and operating discipline to mitigate 
the impact of regulatory and input cost pressures.
Competitive Intensity
Capacity expansion by leading hospital chains is intensifying 
competition across key micro-markets, including Delhi-
NCR, Lucknow, and Mumbai. This may exert pressure on 
pricing, clinician availability, and patient acquisition costs, 
while near-term supply additions in certain clusters could 
affect utilisation.
Response: Strong demand fundamentals, supported by the 
Company’s established brand, clinical capabilities, and focus 
on patient experience, reinforce its competitive position and 
help sustain performance across markets.
Talent Availability and Retention
The persistent shortage of skilled healthcare professionals, 
including doctors, nurses, and allied healthcare staff, remains 
a key industry-wide challenge, particularly in non-metro and 
emerging markets. This may constrain expansion timelines 
and increase recruitment and retention costs.
Response: Continued investment in talent development 
through structured training and academic programmes, 
including DNB courses, along with competitive compensation 
and retention initiatives, strengthens the internal talent 
pipeline and supports the availability of high-quality clinical 
professionals across the Network.
Execution and Ramp-up 
The Company’s ongoing expansion, across brownfield, 
greenfield, and asset-light projects, entails project execution 
and ramp-up risks. Delays in commissioning, insurer 
empanelment and occupancy build-up, along with higher 
initial operating costs for staffing and market development, 
may affect near-term performance. 
Response: The Company’s track record of project execution, 
established presence in key markets, and calibrated ramp-
up approach, supported by institutional demand, help 
mitigate these risks. The Company continues to strengthen 
its execution capabilities through investments in its project 
department and related resources.
Payor and Working Capital Risks
A rising share of insurance and institutional patients is 
altering the revenue mix. Reimbursement delays, claim 
denials, and complex billing and documentation processes 
may lead to deductions, revenue leakage, and delayed 
collections, resulting in higher working capital requirements.
Response: Ongoing enhancements to revenue cycle 
management systems, billing documentation and collection 
processes improve collection efficiency, minimise disputes 
and support liquidity discipline.

Company Outlook
Max Healthcare enters its next phase of growth from a position 
of strength, supported by a robust operating platform, a 
strong expansion pipeline, a healthy balance sheet, and 
disciplined capital allocation. The Company’s ongoing 
brownfield and greenfield expansion projects, asset-light 
growth initiatives, and the ramp-up and integration of recent 
acquisitions and newly commissioned capacities provide 
visibility into medium-term growth, operating leverage, and 
long-term value creation.
The Company’s focus on high-acuity care, improved case 
mix, and an optimised payor mix continues to enhance 
revenue quality and support operating leverage, while 
sustained investment in digital enablement and integrated 
care delivery is strengthening patient engagement and 
clinical throughput.
This balanced approach, combining scale expansion, 
clinical excellence, and capital efficiency, reinforces the 
Company’s leadership position and supports its ability to 
capture emerging opportunities in a structurally strong 
healthcare market.
Risks and Concerns
The Company has established a comprehensive and 
proactive risk management framework to identify, assess 
and mitigate risks that may impact its strategic objectives 
and operational performance. Overseen by the Board of 
Directors, this framework enables structured evaluation 
and continuous monitoring across multiple domains, 
including operational, regulatory, medical, strategic, IT, 
financial, legal and compliance, and human resources. 
The Risk Management Committee (RMC) plays a central 
role in defining the Company’s risk appetite, formulating 
policies, and ensuring their effective implementation across 
the enterprise.
Risks 
are 
reviewed 
regularly 
through 
structured 
engagement with risk owners, self-assessments, detailed 
risk registers, heat maps, and clearly defined mitigation 
plans, with accountability anchored at the senior leadership 
level. While no single risk currently presents an existential 
concern, events such as high-risk litigations, fire incidents, 
or significant regulatory changes could materially affect 
operations and reputation if not managed effectively.
The Company is also exposed to risks associated with the 
integration and operational ramp-up of newly acquired 
hospitals. As digital footprint expands, cyber security and 
data privacy have emerged as critical focus areas, reinforcing 
the need for robust IT governance and strict adherence to 
regulatory requirements.
Internal Financial Control 
Systems and Their Adequacy
The Company has implemented a robust and well-integrated 
internal control framework, supported by advanced IT 
systems and workflow-enabled processes. These controls are 
continuously reviewed and strengthened through periodic 
risk control assessments and testing. A comprehensive 
suite of policies, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and 
guidelines governs all business functions, and is regularly 
updated and made accessible to relevant employees 
through a centralized digital platform, ensuring transparency 
and consistency across the organisation.
The framework is designed to ensure accuracy in financial 
reporting, safeguard assets, and support informed decision-
making. The Internal Audit Plan remains dynamic and aligned 
with the Company’s strategic risks, with audit observations 
and action points closely monitored by the Audit Committee.
During the reporting period, the internal controls were 
assessed and no material weaknesses in design or execution 
were identified. The statutory auditors did not report any 
material weaknesses or mis-statements arising from control 
deficiencies in the course of their audit.

Digital Transformation
Max Healthcare’s digital and AI-led transformation continued 
to strengthen its position as a technology-enabled, patient-
centric healthcare provider during FY 2025–26. Digital 
channels contributed nearly 32% of total revenue during the

The Company strengthened patient access through targeted 
digital interventions. The One Patient One Phone Number

while preserving family-linked profiles. The introduction 
of AI-driven symptom search allows patients to describe 
symptoms in natural language across multiple Indian 
languages and dialects, improving specialist discovery 
and accessibility.
Self-service kiosks and digital interfaces have also redefined 
the patient’s first touchpoint with the hospital, enabling 
registration, appointment booking, and payments, and 
reducing waiting times at the front desk.

Max Healthcare integrated AI across clinical workflows 
during the year. The Pre-OPD Assessment tool generates 
structured clinical summaries by synthesising patient inputs 
with historical records, allowing clinicians to focus on 
consultation rather than documentation. The outpatient EHR 
was upgraded with voice-to-text capture, embedded clinical 
protocols, and contextual decision support.

medical coding engine aligned with ICD-11 standards. The 
underlying MedMax model has demonstrated superior 
accuracy in internal benchmarking at a fraction of 
comparable third-party costs, and has drawn early interest 
from government bodies and insurers - pointing to potential 
external monetisation over time.

Performance Highlights (Standalone)
The Company’s revenue from operations grew by 7.9% to 
₹2,87,445 Lakh in FY 2025-26, compared to ₹2,66,360 Lakh 
in FY 2024-25. Revenue from operations primarily comprises 
of ₹2,59,571 Lakh of revenue from healthcare services, 
₹5,237 Lakh revenue from operation and management 
service fees and ₹15,737 Lakh revenue from the sale 
of pharmaceutical supplies. Other income stood at 
₹30,195 Lakh in FY 2025-26 compared to ₹36,654 Lakh 
in the previous year. The decline is mainly due to lower 
dividend received from wholly owned subsidiaries.
During FY 2025-26, the aggregate of material costs, 
employee expenses, professional fees for doctors, hospital 
services, sales and marketing, power and fuel and other 
overheads - stood at 71.5% of revenue from operations, 
as compared to 68.7% in FY 2024-25. The increase in 
expenditure as a percentage of revenue is primarily 
attributable to the material costs which is up due to 45% 
increase in revenue from sale of drugs and pharmaceuticals 
supplies which typically carry lower margins. Additionally, 
professional and consultancy expenses also rose as a 
percentage of revenue, reﬂecting the Company’s proactive 
strategy to attract and retain clinical talent in anticipation of 
future growth and capacity expansion. Collectively, these 
factors contributed to a 270-basis point increase in direct 
costs and overheads during FY 2025-26.
PBITDA (excluding Other Income) for FY 2025-26 stood at 
₹82,058 Lakh (28.5% of revenue from operations) as 
against ₹83,339 Lakh (31.3% of revenue from operations) in 
FY 2024-25. The moderation in margins reﬂects the 
higher proportion of lower-margin pharmaceutical sales 
and increased investments in clinical talent and operating 
infrastructure to support future growth.
Proﬁt before exceptional item & tax for FY 2025-26 was 
₹93,976 Lakh, compared to ₹1,02,035 Lakh in FY 2024-25, 
representing a decline of 7.9%. The year was impacted by a 
one-time exceptional charge of ₹1,564 Lakh relating to the 
revision of retiral beneﬁt liabilities following the notiﬁcation 
of The Code on Wages, 2019 on November 21, 2025.
Proﬁt After Tax stood at ₹71,661 Lakh, compared to 
₹70,107 Lakh in the previous year reﬂecting a growth of 2.2% 
year on year.
State of Company’s Aﬀairs
The Company continued to scale new heights and has 
successfully laid a strong foundation for all-round growth in 
the future. Its network presently consists of 21 (twenty-one) 
healthcare facilities, including 10 (ten) hospitals and 3 (three) 
medical centres in the Delhi and NCR region. The remaining 
7 (seven) hospitals are located in Mumbai and Nagpur in 
Maharashtra, Mohali and Bathinda in Punjab, Dehradun in 
Uttarakhand, Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh, Bhubaneswar in 
Odisha and 1 (one) medical centre in Mohali. In addition 
to its core hospital business, the network also includes 
two strategic business units (SBUs) - Max@Home and Max 
Lab. Max@Home is a platform that provides health and 
wellness services at home, while Max Lab oﬀers diagnostic 
services to patients outside of its network hospitals. During 
FY 2025-26, the Company divested 2 (two) of its hospitals 
located at Chitta and Anoopshahr pursuant to a strategic 
portfolio review.
The Company, together with its subsidiaries, has further 
strengthened its international footprint and currently 
operates Patient Assistance Centres (“PACs”) across 7 (seven) 
countries, namely Kenya (Nairobi), United Arab Emirates 
(Dubai), Oman (Muscat), Myanmar (Yangon), Uzbekistan 
(Tashkent), Nepal (Kathmandu) and Bangladesh (Dhaka). In 
addition, the Company maintains an indirect presence in 
5 (ﬁve) countries through 5 (ﬁve) partner oﬃces. After closure 
of FY 2025-26, the Company expanded its presence in East 
Africa with the establishment of a new oﬃce in Tanzania 
(Dar es Salaam). The Dubai oﬃce, having completed over 
four years of operations, has established a strong presence 
in the UAE market. The international oﬃces continue to 
engage with local medical tourism facilitators, insurance 
companies, institutional payors such as government bodies 
and hospitals, and individual clinicians to coordinate the 
treatment of patients requiring complex and life-saving 
medical care at the Network Hospitals in India. The 
Company has also taken steps to establish PACs by way of 
an exclusive arrangement with a third-party. These initiatives 
are expected to further strengthen the Company’s position 
as a preferred destination for international patients seeking 
advanced healthcare services. 
The Company continues to maintain a strategic focus on 
organ transplants and other complex surgical procedures 
across its Network Hospitals. It provides medical, operational 
and management services spanning secondary and 
tertiary care specialties, with key areas of focus including 
Oncology, Neurosciences, Cardiac Sciences, Orthopaedics, 
Renal Sciences, and Liver and Biliary Sciences. During 
FY 2025-26, the Company further strengthened its robotic 
surgery programmes across various Network Hospitals and 
successfully performed ~8,600 robotic-assisted procedures, 
underscoring its commitment to advanced clinical care and 
surgical excellence.
In addition to its healthcare operations, the Company also 
generates revenue from pathology, radiology, radiation 
oncology and other allied clinical services. These services 
are oﬀered through fee-for-service and/or revenue-sharing 
arrangements in selected specialties and departments, in 
collaboration with third-party service providers and Partner 
Healthcare Facilities. 
The Company has undertaken several initiatives to 
enhance patient satisfaction, quality of care and clinical 
outcomes, in line with its vision of being the most trusted 
and respected healthcare provider in India. During

The new tower at Nanavati-Max Super Speciality Hospital,

journey. Designed with contemporary architecture and 
state-of-the-art infrastructure, the facility oﬀers enhanced 
patient care capabilities and eﬃcient spatial planning for 
patients, caregivers, and clinical teams. The tower comprises 
15 ﬂoors, including three basement levels, with a total built-
up area of ~7.5 Lakh square feet. 
The 280-bed brownﬁeld expansion tower increases the 
hospital’s existing bed capacity by over 80%. The hospital 
has received Occupancy Certiﬁcate (OC) up to 10th

activities for Phase II of the expansion project, comprising

capacity augmentation plans.

tower, designed to provide a patient-centric environment 
supported by modern aesthetics and premium healthcare 
infrastructure. Following the receipt of the Occupancy 
Certiﬁcate, the hospital commenced patient services from 
the new facility in April 2026.
The 400-bed tower comprises seven ﬂoors, including one 
basement level, a ground ﬂoor, and ﬁve upper ﬂoors, with a 
total built-up area of ~5 Lakh square feet. To date, 156 beds

supporting its long-term growth and expansion objectives.
Construction of Phase-I of Max Super Speciality Hospital, 
Shaheed Path, Lucknow
The Board, at its meeting held on May 21, 2026, approved 
the construction of Phase-I of Max Super Specialty Hospital 
on the 5-acre land parcel owned by the Company located 
at Shaheed Path, Lucknow, with a capacity to accommodate 
~712 census beds. 
Total construction & equipment cost for Phase-I is expected 
to be ~₹1,400 Crore which shall result into blended cost per 
bed of ~₹1.97 Crore (Excluding cost of land).
Existing network hospital at Lucknow had been operating at 
peak occupancy and the additional bed capacity will cater to 
the healthcare needs of communities residing in and around 
Lucknow in State of Uttar Pradesh.
Acquisition of controlling stake in 250 bedded Kalinga 
Hospital Ltd, Bhubaneswar, Odisha 
On May 18, 2026, the Company acquired ~58.28% equity 
stake in Kalinga Hospital Ltd which owns and operates a 
250-bedded multi-speciality hospital under the brand name 
‘Kalinga Hospital’ at Bhubaneswar, Odisha. 
The acquisition marks the Company’s entry into the Eastern 
India healthcare market and strengthens its network 
by adding a well-established hospital in a strategically 
important region, thereby expanding the Company’s 
geographical footprint.
The acquisition of controlling stake for an aggregate 
consideration of ₹297.97 Crore was funded through an 
External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) facility availed from 
Standard Chartered Bank.
Other Events:

Pursuant to the approval of the Renewable Energy 
Investment Committee at its meeting held on July 1, 2025, 
the Company acquired the equity shares of Yogindera 
Powers Limited (“YPL”). The investment is intended to enable 
Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket (West) and Max Super 
Speciality Hospital, Shalimar Bagh to procure captive green 
power, thereby driving cost eﬃciencies and supporting 
the Company’s Environmental, Social and Governance 
(ESG) objectives through a reduced carbon footprint. As on 
March 31, 2026, the Company held 8,66,945 equity shares of 
₹10 each of YPL, representing 16.64% of its issued equity 
share capital.

purchase agreement for procurement of solar power. The

Divestment of hospitals located at Chitta and Anoopshahr
During FY 2025-26, the Board of Crosslay Remedies Limited 
(CRL) (formerly Jaypee Healthcare Limited), a wholly-owned 
subsidiary of the Company, approved the divestment of its 
hospitals located at Chitta and Anoopshahr pursuant to a 
strategic portfolio review. 
Anoopshahr Hospital was non-operational and required 
signiﬁcant capital expenditure with no viable business case 
for revival, while Chitta Hospital had been incurring continued 
operational losses and faced infrastructure, manpower and 
cost challenges, including projected losses of ~₹10 Crore. 
Considering these factors and associated operational risks, 
CRL divested both hospitals for an aggregate consideration 
of ~₹40 Crore, to enable focused allocation of resources to 
higher priority assets.
